cards.text: This one's a psalm of the sons of Korah, written for the choirmaster. And it opens LOUD, calling every people and everyone living in the world to listen up. Friend, that's the biggest group chat ever started, and NOBODY gets to mute it.

cards.question: True or false: the writer says this message is for the rich, so the poor can skip it.

cards.text: Then the writer promises wisdom from his mouth and understanding from his heart. He's got a proverb and a riddle, and he's not just going to say it. He's going to PLAY it.

cards.question: The writer has a riddle to share, and he's going to play it. What will he express it with?

cards.text: So here's the riddle. Trouble's here and wicked usurpers surround him, and he asks why he should be afraid.

cards.question: The wicked usurpers surrounding the writer are leaning hard on something. What do they trust in?

cards.text: Yep, they trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches. Me? Never had that problem, friend, because my WHOLE price tag was 25 cents.

cards.question: True or false: with enough money, a man can redeem his brother by paying his ransom to God.

cards.text: The redemption of a soul is costly, and no payment would ever be enough. That's a price tag even the guy who mentions his boat in EVERY conversation can't cover.

cards.question: No payment could ever be enough to redeem a soul. What would that payment be trying to buy?

answers.text: A seat in the king's own court

cards.text: Now look around, friend. The writer says it's clear that the wise man and the fool end up the same way.

cards.question: The writer says it's clear that wise men ___ just like the foolish and the senseless.
When the foolish and the senseless perish, what happens to all their wealth?

cards.text: Some of these folks even had their lands named after them. The Millers carved my name on a handle, and I STILL ended up in a junk drawer.

cards.question: Their lands carried their names, but the writer says their ___ are their eternal homes.
True or false: the writer says that despite his wealth, a man cannot endure.

cards.text: All that wealth, and he still can't endure. The writer says he's like the beasts that perish.
The writer looks back at everything he just said and calls it the fate of the foolish. Then, Selah.

cards.question: True or false: the writer says this fate is for the foolish only, and not for the followers who endorse their sayings.

cards.text: Then he paints a picture, and it gets DARK. The foolish are like sheep, destined for Sheol.

cards.question: The foolish are like sheep destined for Sheol. Who does the writer say will be their shepherd?

cards.text: Death as their shepherd. Friend, that is one flock you do NOT want to join, no matter how green the grass looks.

cards.question: The writer says that in the morning, the ___ will rule over the foolish.

cards.text: Their form decays in Sheol, far from their lofty abode. Then the writer drops one little word that flips the whole psalm: But.

cards.question: No man can pay God a ransom for a life. So who does the writer say will redeem HIS life from Sheol?
True or false: the writer says God will surely take him to Himself.

cards.text: God will surely take him to Himself, and then, Selah. Somebody reached into a dark junk drawer for me once, friend, so this line gets me EVERY time.
Then the writer turns to the listener with some advice about that neighbor whose house keeps getting fancier.

cards.question: True or false: the writer says to be afraid when a man grows rich and the splendor of his house increases.
So why shouldn't you be afraid when a man grows rich?

answers.text: When he dies he carries nothing away
His riches will soon be stolen from him
He will lose it all before he grows old

cards.text: His abundance will not follow him down. Friend, I have NEVER seen a moving truck following a hearse.
In his lifetime he blesses his own soul. And the writer adds that men praise you when you prosper.

cards.question: The rich man blessed himself and soaked up the praise. But when he dies, who does he join?
In the last line, the man who is like the beasts that perish is the one with riches but without ___.

cards.text: His fathers will never see the light of day. And the psalm closes with that beasts-that-perish line from earlier, now aimed at riches without understanding.

findings.problem: This is not the opening card, but it has three sentences: 'Then the writer promises wisdom...', 'He's got a proverb and a riddle, and he's not just going to say it.', and 'He's going to PLAY it.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The question asks the baker to guess a detail of the line (harp, trumpet or tambourine). The baker can't reason it out, which matches the Psalm 23 'anoint with oil' bad example. Card 3's hint 'He's going to PLAY it' fits all three answers, so the baker can only get it by luck.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'Yep, they trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches.', 'Me?' and 'Never had that problem, friend, because my WHOLE price tag was 25 cents.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This card only repeats the answer to card 4 ('Death as their shepherd') and adds a joke. It tells no new part of Psalm 49:14, so it is a recap card.
The card tells the word 'But', which opens Psalm 49:15, but it cites only Psalm 49:14. The citation should be Psalm 49:14-15.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The card says the advice in Psalm 49:16 is about 'that neighbor whose house keeps getting fancier.' The text says 'a man' and never calls him a neighbor. The card presents this as what the writer says, not as Papa Dorin's own comparison.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: Card 17 has already asked about Psalm 49:20. This last card then goes back to the end of Psalm 49:19 ('never see the light of day') and repeats the Psalm 49:20 line, which card 17 already showed. The passage moves backward, and part of the card is a recap.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.
